from pypdf import PdfReader

r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(r.pages))

texts=[]

    t=p.extract_text()
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n{t}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts))

strengths: The controlled instance-classification paradigm meaningfully separates fully seen objects from partially seen objects and holds total training-set size fixed while varying their proportions. This enables a useful investigation of orientation generalization.

The per-orientation heatmaps reveal structured successes and failures that aggregate accuracy obscures. The concentration of generalization near familiar views and their in-plane rotations is an informative empirical finding for researchers studying visual robustness and representations.

The experiments include three object families, multiple seed-orientation distributions, cross-category conditions, several architectures, five repetitions, and pretraining, augmentation, and reduced-data controls. These provide substantial support for the descriptive findings within the tested setting.

The experimental paradigm is generally understandable, the geometric model is interpretable, and the manuscript provides training details and code/data links. The work has an identifiable interested audience without needing a new architecture or state-of-the-art results.
weaknesses: Necessary: Validate what the invariance metric measures (Sec. 2.5, Eqs. 5–8). Equal average activations over two orientation sets do not establish invariant responses across individual orientations: substantial view dependence can disappear through averaging. Furthermore, requiring activity above the 95th-percentile threshold in both sets excludes neurons that respond strongly in-distribution but lose their response out-of-distribution. The resulting conditional average can therefore conceal failures of invariance. Report a complementary analysis preserving orientation-level variation, select units independently of their OoD responses, and report retained-pair counts and threshold sensitivity; alternatively, narrow the interpretation to similarity of selected mean responses.

Necessary: Resolve an apparent inconsistency in the generalizable/non-generalizable partition. Sec. 2.5 thresholds the fitted predictor at 10% of its maximum, but the predictor is an uncalibrated sum of logistic components, fitted using Pearson correlation. The scores around 1.8–2.4 displayed in Fig. S9c would all exceed that cutoff. Specify any omitted normalization and reconcile the plotted scores with the stated procedure. This matters because the partition underlies the neural analyses and Fig. S8; its robustness cannot be assumed.

Necessary: Distinguish descriptive fitting from predictive validation (Sec. 2.4 and Fig. 4). The model parameters are optimized against the correlation subsequently reported, and no separate fitting/evaluation split is described. Consequently, the reported correlations above 0.8 establish goodness of fit, rather than demonstrated prediction on held-out orientations or experiments. Either provide independent evaluation or consistently describe the model as a fitted characterization. Because this fitted model also defines the downstream orientation groups, their accuracy separation is not independent validation of the partitioning rules.

Necessary: Align the mechanistic conclusions with the evidence (Secs. 3.3–4). The correlations between accuracy, fully-seen invariance, and partially-seen invariance are compatible with dissemination through shared features, but do not identify its direction or establish that particular neurons mediate the effect. Similar aggregate scores can also arise from common image geometry and joint training. Although the abstract presents a hypothesis, later statements that generalization is 'driven by' dissemination and that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs are stronger. Retain these as hypotheses unless supported by targeted interventions or controls that distinguish the proposed mechanism from alternatives.

Optional improvements: Specify the Euler rotation convention, orientation-sampling distribution, cubelet resolution, and evaluation samples per cell more explicitly. Numerical correlations stratified by architecture and seed would help interpret Fig. 5, while larger labels would improve the dense quantitative figures. Broader natural-image experiments would extend applicability, but are not necessary for publishing appropriately bounded findings.
